items.title: The Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) Dynasty & Thanesar
items.body:
### The Pushyabhuti dynasty and Thanesar

**In one line**
Harshavardhana belonged to the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty, which ruled a small north-Indian kingdom from Thanesar.

**Why it is asked**
A common one-mark question is simply "which dynasty / which seat?" — and students confuse Harsha's Pushyabhuti line with the Maukharis of Kannauj.

**The story**
**Harshavardhana** (usually called **Harsha**) was born in **590 CE at Thanesar** (Sanskrit *Sthanvishvara*), a town in present-day **Haryana**. His family, the **Pushyabhuti dynasty** — also called the **Vardhana dynasty** because the kings' names end in *-vardhana* — ruled only a **small kingdom** in northern India at first. His father **Prabhakarvardhan** was the ruler of Thanesar, and his elder brother **Rajyavardhan** was the crown prince. Thanesar was the dynasty's early seat; Harsha would later move the political centre to the great city of **Kannauj**.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Dynasty | Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) |
| Original seat | Thanesar (Sthanvishvara), Haryana |
| Father | Prabhakarvardhan |
| Elder brother | Rajyavardhan (crown prince) |
| Later capital | Kannauj |

**Terms explained**
- **Pushyabhuti / Vardhana dynasty** — Harsha's royal family; the two names mean the same line.
- **Sthanvishvara** — the Sanskrit name of Thanesar, the family's home town.

**Don't confuse**
The **Pushyabhutis** (Harsha's family, at Thanesar) with the **Maukharis** (a separate dynasty at Kannauj, into which Harsha's sister married). Harsha later *united* the two realms.

**Remember it**
"Pushyabhuti = Vardhana; Thanesar first, Kannauj later."

**TL;DR**
- Harsha was born in 590 CE at Thanesar (Haryana).
- His dynasty was the Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) line.
- Father Prabhakarvardhan ruled Thanesar; brother Rajyavardhan was crown prince.
- The seat was Thanesar at first; the capital later shifted to Kannauj.

figure.caption: The Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) ruler Harshavardhana and the extent of his empire, seated originally at Thanesar (Sthanvishvara).

keyPoints: Harsha born 590 CE at Thanesar (Sthanvishvara), present-day Haryana.
Belonged to the Pushyabhuti dynasty, also called the Vardhana dynasty.
Father Prabhakarvardhan ruled Thanesar; elder brother Rajyavardhan was crown prince.
Dynasty's original seat was Thanesar; capital later shifted to Kannauj.

items.title: Harsha's Rise (606 CE) & the Harsha Era
items.body:
### Harsha's rise and the Harsha era

**In one line**
Harsha came to the throne at just sixteen in 606 CE, a year taken as the start of the Harsha era.

**Why it is asked**
The date 606 CE and the "Harsha era" are exact facts the exam loves, and the tragic back-story (two deaths) is a favourite link.

**The story**
Harsha did not expect to rule. His father died, and then his elder brother **Rajyavardhan was killed** and his sister's husband, the Maukhari king **Grahavarman, was assassinated**. With the throne suddenly empty, Harsha ascended at the young age of **16, in about 606 CE**. At first his power was limited to the **small kingdom of Thanesar**, but he quickly set out to **unite northern India**. His accession in **606 CE** is traditionally taken as the start of the **Harsha era (Harshabda)**, a system of counting years used in later inscriptions. He grew into a capable soldier and administrator who built one of the last great empires of the north.

**Picture it**

| Event | When |
|---|---|
| Birth at Thanesar | 590 CE |
| Deaths of Rajyavardhan and Grahavarman | shortly before 606 CE |
| Accession at age 16 (Harsha era begins) | c. 606 CE |

**Terms explained**
- **Harsha era (Harshabda)** — a calendar counted from Harsha's accession in 606 CE.
- **Accession** — the act of coming to the throne.

**Don't confuse**
The **Harsha era (606 CE)** with the earlier **Gupta era (c. 319 CE)** or the **Shaka era (78 CE)**. Different starting kings, different years.

**Remember it**
"606 = Sixteen and Sovereign" — Harsha is crowned and the Harsha era begins.

**TL;DR**
- Harsha ascended the Thanesar throne at 16, c. 606 CE.
- His rise followed the death of brother Rajyavardhan and the murder of Grahavarman.
- 606 CE marks the start of the Harsha era (Harshabda).
- He began confined to Thanesar but aimed to unite the north.
keyPoints: Ascended the Thanesar throne at age 16, c. 606 CE.
Rise followed the death of brother Rajyavardhan and murder of Grahavarman.
606 CE marks the start of the Harsha era (Harshabda).
Began confined to Thanesar but aimed to unite northern India.
items.mnemonic: '606 = Sixteen & Sovereign' — Harsha crowned, Harsha era begins.

items.title: Political Expansion — From Thanesar to Kannauj
items.body:
### Political expansion to Kannauj

**In one line**
Harsha avenged his family by defeating Shashanka, then united Thanesar with Kannauj and spread his power across the north.

**Why it is asked**
The chain "Shashanka → Bhaskaravarman alliance → Kannauj capital" is high-yield, and the exam tests who Harsha allied with and whom he fought.

**The story**
Harsha's **first campaign was against Shashanka of Gauda** (the king of Bengal), who had killed his brother Rajyavardhan and whose action had led to the kidnapping of Harsha's sister **Rajyashri**. Harsha allied with **Bhaskaravarman, the king of Kamarupa (Assam)** in the east, and together they defeated Shashanka. Harsha then **claimed Kannauj** (whose Maukhari throne had fallen vacant), **united Thanesar and Kannauj**, and made **Kannauj his capital**. From there he brought many smaller kingdoms under his overlordship: he controlled **Punjab and central India**, **annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha**, and **defeated the Vallabhi king in Gujarat**, extending his influence to the west.

**Picture it**

| Step | What happened |
|---|---|
| First war | against Shashanka of Gauda (Bengal) |
| Key ally | Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa (Assam) |
| Capital | Kannauj (united with Thanesar) |
| Annexed | Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; Punjab and central India held |
| West | defeated the Vallabhi king (Gujarat) |

**Terms explained**
- **Gauda** — the kingdom of Bengal, ruled by Shashanka.
- **Kamarupa** — the ancient kingdom of Assam, ruled by Harsha's ally Bhaskaravarman.
- **Vallabhi** — a kingdom in the Saurashtra region of Gujarat.

**Don't confuse**
**Shashanka** (enemy, of Gauda/Bengal) with **Bhaskaravarman** (ally, of Kamarupa/Assam). The exam deliberately swaps them.

**Remember it**
"Shashanka first, then Kannauj capital — Bengal, Bihar, Odisha and Vallabhi."

**TL;DR**
- First campaign was against Shashanka of Gauda; Harsha allied with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa.
- He united Thanesar and Kannauj and made Kannauj his capital.
- He held Punjab and central India and annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.
- He also defeated the Vallabhi king in Gujarat.

figure.alt: Detailed map of Harshavardhana's empire 606 CE to 647 CE with capital Kannauj, Sthanvishvara, Magadha and the Narmada boundary
figure.caption: Harshavardhana's empire (606–647 CE): capital at Kannauj, spanning the Ganges plains up to the Narmada in the south.

keyPoints: First campaign against Shashanka of Gauda; allied with Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa.
United Thanesar and Kannauj; made Kannauj his capital.
Controlled Punjab and central India; annexed Bengal, Bihar and Odisha.
Defeated the Vallabhi king in Gujarat.
items.mnemonic: Shashanka first, then Kannauj capital — 'Bengal-Bihar-Odisha + Vallabhi'.

items.title: Defeat by Pulakeshin II & the Narmada Boundary
items.body:
### Defeat by Pulakeshin II

**In one line**
The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha, fixing the Narmada River as the boundary between north and south.

**Why it is asked**
This is the single most tested fact about Harsha — and often set as an assertion-reason, where the date is the trap.

**The story**
Harsha was unbeaten in the north, but when he turned **south towards the Deccan** he met his match. The **Chalukya king Pulakeshin II**, ruling from **Vatapi (Badami)**, **defeated Harsha in 618–619 CE** and forced him to retreat. As a result, Harsha's southern limit was fixed at the **Narmada River**, which became the effective boundary between the two powers. The victory is celebrated in Pulakeshin's **Aihole inscription** (composed by Ravikirti). Note on the date: a Chalukya grant of **4 April 619 CE** already mentions this victory, so the battle is now dated to the **winter of 618–619 CE** — the older guess of "around 630 CE" is no longer accepted.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Winner | Pulakeshin II (Chalukya) |
| Chalukya capital | Vatapi (Badami) |
| Date | 618–619 CE |
| Result | Narmada River = Harsha's southern limit |
| Record | Aihole inscription (by Ravikirti) |

**Terms explained**
- **Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami)** — the leading Deccan dynasty of the 7th century.
- **Aihole inscription** — a prashasti of Pulakeshin II that records his win over Harsha.

**Don't confuse**
The assertion "Narmada was Harsha's southern limit" (true) with any **wrong date** attached as the reason. The correct, modern date is 618–619 CE.

**Remember it**
"Pulakeshin pushed Harsha back to the Narmada" — the south stayed Chalukya.

**TL;DR**
- Harsha failed to expand into the south.
- Pulakeshin II of Vatapi defeated him in 618–619 CE.
- The defeat fixed Harsha's southern limit at the Narmada River.
- The win is recorded in Pulakeshin's Aihole inscription.
keyPoints: Harsha failed to expand into the south of India.
Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha in 618–619 CE.
The defeat fixed Harsha's southern limit at the Narmada River.
Pulakeshin II's Chalukya capital was Vatapi (Badami); the Aihole inscription records the victory.
items.mnemonic: 'Pulakeshin pushed Harsha back to the Narmada' — south stayed Chalukya.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Political expansion; Contemporary Kingdoms); Wikipedia on Pulakeshin II (618–619 CE from the Bijapur-Mumbai grant)

items.title: Banabhatta — Harshacharita & Kadambari
items.body:
### Banabhatta, the court poet

**In one line**
Banabhatta was Harsha's court poet, author of the Harshacharita (a verse life of Harsha) and the Kadambari.

**Why it is asked**
Author-to-work matching is a staple, and Banabhatta's two works are repeatedly tested.

**The story**
**Banabhatta** (active about **606 to 647 CE**) was a **poet at Harsha's court** and one of the great masters of Sanskrit prose. His chief work, the **Harshacharita** ("Deeds of Harsha"), is a **biography of the king written in verse** and is often called the first historical biography in Sanskrit. He also wrote the **Kadambari**, a romance regarded as **one of the world's earliest novels**. Banabhatta is the most famous of the many artists and scholars drawn to Harsha's generous court.

**Picture it**

| Work | What it is |
|---|---|
| Harshacharita | verse biography of Harsha ('Deeds of Harsha') |
| Kadambari | prose romance, one of the earliest novels |

**Terms explained**
- **Harshacharita** — "the deeds/life of Harsha"; a court biography and key historical source.
- **Kadambari** — a long prose romance named after its heroine.

**Don't confuse**
**Banabhatta** (Harsha's poet; Harshacharita, Kadambari) with **Harsha himself** (who wrote the *plays* Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda). The king and his poet wrote different works.

**Remember it**
"Bana wrote two: Harshacharita (life) and Kadambari (novel)."

**TL;DR**
- Banabhatta (c. 606–647 CE) was a poet in Harsha's court.
- The Harshacharita is a verse biography of Harsha.
- The Kadambari is one of the world's earliest novels.
- Harsha's patronage drew many artists; Banabhatta was the most celebrated.
keyPoints: Banabhatta (c. 606–647 CE) was a poet in Harsha's court.
Harshacharita = biography of Harsha ('Deeds of Harsha'), written in verse.
Kadambari = one of the world's earliest novels.
Harsha's patronage of art and literature drew many artists to his court.

items.title: Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) & the Si-Yu-Ki
items.body:
### Hiuen-Tsang and the Si-Yu-Ki

**In one line**
Hiuen-Tsang was the Chinese pilgrim whose travel account, the Si-Yu-Ki, is our richest source on Harsha's India.

**Why it is asked**
The pairing "Hiuen-Tsang ↔ Harsha ↔ Si-Yu-Ki" is near-certain, and he is routinely contrasted with Fa-Hien (Gupta age) and I-Tsing (later).

**The story**
**Hiuen-Tsang (also spelt Xuanzang)** was a **Chinese Buddhist pilgrim** who spent nearly **13 years in India (630 to 643 CE)** during Harsha's reign. He came to collect **sacred texts and relics** to carry back to China, and visited sites linked to the Buddha's life — which earned him the nickname the **"prince of pilgrims"**. His book, the **Si-Yu-Ki** ("Records of the Western World"), describes the **social, economic, religious and cultural** life of the age in detail. He recorded that **Nalanda** was the leading university, that **Prayag and Kanauj** were rising centres while **Pataliputra and Vaishali** had declined, and — honestly — that **he himself was robbed once**, showing that law and order were not perfect.

**Picture it**

| Pilgrim | Era | King | Work |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fa-Hien | Gupta (c. 399–414 CE) | Chandragupta II | travelogue |
| Hiuen-Tsang | 630–643 CE | Harshavardhana | Si-Yu-Ki |
| I-Tsing | 671–695 CE | after Harsha | monk biographies |

**Terms explained**
- **Si-Yu-Ki** — Hiuen-Tsang's account of his Indian travels.
- **Pilgrim** — a religious traveller; he came to study and collect Buddhist scriptures.

**Don't confuse**
**Hiuen-Tsang** (under Harsha, 7th century) with **Fa-Hien** (under Chandragupta II, 5th century) and **I-Tsing** (671–695 CE, after Harsha). Three different Chinese travellers, three different reigns.

**Remember it**
"Xuanzang = prince of pilgrims, 13 years (630–643), wrote the Si-Yu-Ki."

**TL;DR**
- Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) was in India c. 630–643 CE (~13 years) during Harsha's reign.
- He wrote the Si-Yu-Ki, our key source on Harsha's society.
- He was called the 'prince of pilgrims'.
- He praised Nalanda; noted Prayag and Kanauj rising, Pataliputra and Vaishali declining.
keyPoints: Hiuen-Tsang (Xuanzang) was a Chinese pilgrim in India c. 630–643 CE (~13 years).
Wrote the Si-Yu-Ki, a key source on Harsha's social/economic/religious life.
Called the 'prince of pilgrims'; came to visit Buddhist sites.
Noted Nalanda as the leading university; Prayag & Kanauj rising, Pataliputra & Vaishali declining.
items.mnemonic: Xuanzang = 'Prince of Pilgrims', 13 years (630–643), wrote Si-Yu-Ki.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Hiuen Tsang's Si-Yu-Ki)

items.title: Patronage of Nalanda & Education
items.body:
### Nalanda and education under Harsha

**In one line**
Nalanda was the leading university of Harsha's day, and higher learning was based in monasteries with Sanskrit as its language.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests "Nalanda = top university under Harsha" and the features of the education system Hiuen-Tsang described.

**The story**
In Hiuen-Tsang's account, **Nalanda** was the **leading educational university** of the time, and **Harsha was one of its major patrons**. **Education was given in the monasteries** and was largely **religious** in character, producing a great body of religious literature. The **Vedas were taught orally** (passed on by memory, not written down), and **Sanskrit was the language of the learned**. A student's formal learning usually ran **from about age 9 to age 30**, and many scholars devoted their whole lives to study; wandering monks (*bhikkhus*) and ascetics (*sadhus*) were respected for their learning.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Top university | Nalanda (patronised by Harsha) |
| Where taught | monasteries (mostly religious study) |
| Vedas | taught orally, not written |
| Scholarly language | Sanskrit |
| Age of study | roughly 9 to 30 |

**Terms explained**
- **Monastery (vihara)** — a residence of monks that doubled as a teaching centre.
- **Oral tradition** — knowledge passed on by memory and recitation rather than writing.

**Don't confuse**
**Nalanda** (flourished under the Guptas, Harsha and the Palas) with **Vikramshila** (founded later, in the Pala period) and **Taxila** (famous in a much earlier age). All are ancient centres of learning, from different periods.

**Remember it**
"Nalanda = No. 1 university" under Harsha's patronage.

**TL;DR**
- Nalanda was the leading university, patronised by Harsha.
- Education was monastery-based and largely religious.
- The Vedas were taught orally; Sanskrit was the scholarly language.
- Study spanned roughly ages 9 to 30.
keyPoints: Nalanda was the leading educational university, patronised by Harsha.
Education was monastery-based and largely religious.
Vedas taught orally; Sanskrit was the language of the learned.
Learning spanned ages 9–30; the I-Tsing biographies describe Nalanda's monks.
items.mnemonic: 'Nalanda = No.1 university' — Harsha's great educational patronage.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Education; Hiuen Tsang's observations; I-Tsing)

items.title: The Kannauj & Prayag Assemblies
items.body:
### The Kannauj and Prayag assemblies

**In one line**
Harsha held two famous religious gatherings — one at Kannauj honouring Hiuen-Tsang, and a great charity assembly at Prayag.

**Why it is asked**
The exam asks "where did Harsha hold his assemblies?" and tests the Kannauj (Buddhist) versus Prayag (charity) distinction.

**The story**
Under Harsha, **Prayag and Kanauj** became the empire's chief **religious and cultural centres** (as the old cities of Pataliputra and Vaishali declined). Harsha convened a grand **assembly at Kannauj** (around 643 CE) to honour the pilgrim **Hiuen-Tsang** and to promote **Mahayana Buddhism**; it was attended by kings, monks and scholars. He is even more famous for the **assembly at Prayag** (modern Allahabad/Prayagraj), a **quinquennial** gathering — held roughly **every five years** — at which the king gave away the royal treasury as **alms (dana)**. These assemblies show Harsha's **secular patronage**: although he leaned towards Buddhism, he honoured all faiths.

**Picture it**

| Assembly | Place | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Kannauj | Kannauj | honour Hiuen-Tsang; promote Mahayana Buddhism |
| Prayag | Prayag (Allahabad) | great charity (dana) every ~5 years |

**Terms explained**
- **Quinquennial** — happening once every five years (the Prayag assembly).
- **Dana** — the religious giving away of wealth as charity.

**Don't confuse**
The **Kannauj assembly** (Buddhist, for Hiuen-Tsang) with the **Prayag assembly** (charity, every five years). Both are Harsha's, but with different purposes.

**Remember it**
"Two assemblies — Kannauj for the pilgrim, Prayag for charity."

**TL;DR**
- Prayag and Kanauj were the key religious and cultural centres under Harsha.
- The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen-Tsang and promoted Mahayana Buddhism.
- The Prayag assembly was a great charitable gathering held about every five years.
- The assemblies reflect Harsha's secular, all-faith patronage.
keyPoints: Prayag and Kanauj were the key religious/cultural centres under Harsha.
The Kannauj assembly honoured Hiuen-Tsang and promoted Mahayana Buddhism.
The Prayag assembly was a great charitable convocation of alms-giving every ~5 years.
The assemblies show Harsha's secular, all-faith patronage.
items.mnemonic: Two assemblies — 'Kannauj for the pilgrim, Prayag for charity'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: The Reign of Harshavardhana (Hiuen Tsang's observations — Prayag & Kanauj as centres; religion)

items.title: Harsha the Author — Nagananda, Ratnavali & Priyadarshika
items.body:
### Harsha as a playwright

**In one line**
Harsha was not only a king but an author who wrote three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests "which three plays did Harsha write?" and traps students by mixing in works by Banabhatta or Vishakhadatta.

**The story**
Harsha was himself a **noted scholar and author** who wrote **three Sanskrit plays**. **Ratnavali** ("Precious Garland") is a romance about a beautiful princess, **Ratnavali**, and King **Udayana**; it has **four acts** and contains an early reference to the **festival of colours, Holi**. **Priyadarshika** is another court romance. **Nagananda** is famous for its **Buddhist theme** (the self-sacrifice of prince Jimutavahana), reflecting Harsha's Buddhist leaning. His authorship, alongside the work of poets like Banabhatta, made his court a high point of Sanskrit literature.

**Picture it**

| Play | Note |
|---|---|
| Ratnavali | princess Ratnavali and King Udayana; four acts; early Holi reference |
| Priyadarshika | a court romance |
| Nagananda | Buddhist theme (Jimutavahana) |

**Terms explained**
- **Nagananda** — Harsha's Buddhist-themed play about self-sacrifice.
- **Udayana** — the legendary king who is the hero of Ratnavali.

**Don't confuse**
Harsha's **plays** (Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda) with Banabhatta's **prose** (Harshacharita, Kadambari), and with Vishakhadatta's **Mudrarakshasa** (a Gupta-age play, a classic trap).

**Remember it**
"N-R-P: Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarshika — Harsha's three plays."

**TL;DR**
- Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.
- Ratnavali is a four-act romance of princess Ratnavali and King Udayana, with an early Holi reference.
- Nagananda carries a Buddhist theme.
- Harsha was both patron and author in a golden court of letters.
keyPoints: Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays: Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda.
Ratnavali ('Precious Garland') — princess Ratnavali and King Udayana, in four acts.
Ratnavali contains an early reference to Holi, the festival of colours.
Nagananda carries a Buddhist theme; Harsha was both patron and author.
items.mnemonic: 'N-R-P' — Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarshika: Harsha's three plays.

items.title: Administration, Revenue & Feudalism
items.body:
### Administration, revenue and feudalism

**In one line**
Harsha ruled through a layered, increasingly feudal administration funded by three main taxes, with so much paid in land grants that few coins were issued.

**Why it is asked**
The exam matches officials to posts, taxes to their nature, and asks why Harsha issued few coins.

**The story**
Harsha kept **strong central authority** but his polity was increasingly **feudalised and decentralised**. The empire was divided into provinces (**Bhuktis**) under **Governors**, districts (**Vishayas**) under **Vishayapatis**, and villages under headmen (**Gramikas**). He was advised by a **Mantri Parishad (Council of Ministers)**; among the key officials were **Avanti** (foreign relations and war), **Simhanada** (Commander-in-Chief), **Kuntala** (cavalry) and **Skandagupta** (chief of the elephant force). A large army — reportedly about **100,000 cavalry, 50,000 infantry and 60,000 elephants** — upheld his rule.

Revenue came mainly from **three taxes**: **Bhaga** (the land tax, one-sixth of the produce), **Hiranya** (a tax paid in cash by farmers and merchants) and **Bali** (an additional, often oppressive levy). Importantly, officers and religious figures were often paid with **grants of land (Agraharas)** rather than in cash — which **spread feudalism** and is why **Harsha issued very few coins**.

**Picture it**

| Tax | What it was |
|---|---|
| Bhaga | land tax, one-sixth (1/6) of the produce |
| Hiranya | tax paid in cash by farmers and merchants |
| Bali | an additional, oppressive levy |

**Terms explained**
- **Agrahara** — a tax-free grant of land, usually to Brahmins or religious bodies.
- **Feudalism** — a system where power and revenue pass to local land-holding lords.
- **Mantri Parishad** — the king's Council of Ministers.

**Don't confuse**
**Bhaga** (land tax, a *share* of produce) with **Hiranya** (a *cash* tax). The names are easy to swap.

**Remember it**
Taxes "B-H-B": Bhaga (land share), Hiranya (cash), Bali (extra).

**TL;DR**
- Structure: Bhukti (Governor) → Vishaya (Vishayapati) → Grama (Gramika); advised by a Mantri Parishad.
- Officials: Avanti (war/foreign), Simhanada (C-in-C), Kuntala (cavalry), Skandagupta (elephants).
- Three taxes: Bhaga (land, 1/6), Hiranya (cash), Bali (additional).
- Land grants (Agraharas) spread feudalism, so Harsha issued few coins; large army of cavalry, infantry and elephants.
keyPoints: Provinces = Bhuktis (Governors); districts = Vishayas (Vishayapatis); villages under Gramikas.
Assisted by a Mantri Parishad; Avanti (war/foreign), Simhanada (C-in-C), Skandagupta (elephants).
Three taxes: Bhaga (land, 1/6 produce), Hiranya (cash), Bali (additional).
Land grants (Agraharas) spread feudalism; few coins issued; huge army of cavalry, infantry & elephants.

items.title: Decline & Legacy of Harsha's Empire
items.body:
### Decline and legacy

**In one line**
Harsha's empire broke up soon after his heirless death in 647 CE, but he is remembered as the last great ruler of northern India before the Islamic invasions.

**Why it is asked**
The exam tests the death year (647 CE), the cause of collapse (no heir plus feudatories), and Harsha's place in history.

**The story**
Harsha's empire began to **decline after his death in 647 CE**. Because he **left no heir**, the feudatory kings and land-holding nobles he had relied on broke away, and the empire **disintegrated into smaller regional kingdoms**. Yet his reign is remembered as a generation of **peace, prosperity and cultural achievement**, and he stands as **one of the last great rulers of northern India** before the coming of Islamic power. His **patronage of the arts and of Nalanda University**, together with his own writings and the records of Banabhatta and Hiuen-Tsang, secured him a lasting place in India's intellectual history.

**Picture it**

| Point | Detail |
|---|---|
| Death | 647 CE |
| Heir | none |
| Result | empire splits into regional kingdoms |
| Legacy | last great northern emperor; patron of arts and Nalanda |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory** — a subordinate ruler who breaks away when central power weakens.
- **Heirless** — leaving no successor, so no clear claimant to the throne.

**Don't confuse**
The collapse of **Harsha's empire (647 CE, no heir)** with the fall of the **Guptas** (a century earlier, by Huna invasions and feudalisation). Both ended in fragmentation, but by different triggers.

**Remember it**
"647 and no heir" — the empire splinters; Harsha is the last great northern emperor.

**TL;DR**
- Harsha's empire declined after his death in 647 CE.
- He left no heir, so it broke into smaller regional kingdoms.
- He is remembered as one of the last great rulers of northern India before Islamic invasions.
- His legacy is cultural: patronage of the arts and Nalanda, in an age of peace and prosperity.
keyPoints: Empire declined after Harsha's death in 647 CE; he left no heirs.
It disintegrated into smaller regional kingdoms (feudatories).
Remembered as one of the last great rulers of northern India before Islamic invasions.
Legacy: patronage of arts and Nalanda University; an age of peace and prosperity.

items.title: For Mains — Harshavardhana
items.body:
### For Mains — Harshavardhana as an analytical theme

**In one line**
For Mains, present Harsha as the last attempt at pan-north-Indian empire before early-medieval fragmentation, and weigh his cultural glory against the feudalising forces that doomed his state.

**The dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Rise and unification | Pushyabhuti base at Thanesar; avenging Rajyavardhan; Bhaskaravarman alliance; Thanesar + Kannauj united under one capital |
| Limits of power | checked at the Narmada by Pulakeshin II (618–619 CE); never held the Deccan or the far south |
| Cultural achievement | Harsha's own plays (Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda); Banabhatta (Harshacharita, Kadambari); patronage of Nalanda; Kannauj and Prayag assemblies |
| Administration and economy | Mantri Parishad; Bhukti-Vishaya-Grama; taxes Bhaga/Hiranya/Bali; land grants (Agraharas) and few coins |
| Nature and decline | personal, quasi-feudal paramountcy over feudatories; heirless death in 647 CE → disintegration |

**Data points and names to quote**
- Dates: reign c. 606–647 CE; Harsha era from 606 CE; Pulakeshin defeat 618–619 CE; Hiuen-Tsang in India 630–643 CE.
- Sources: Banabhatta's Harshacharita; Hiuen-Tsang's Si-Yu-Ki; Pulakeshin's Aihole inscription (Ravikirti).
- Debate: was Harsha's state a centralised empire or a loose feudal paramountcy? Cite the land-grant economy and the few coins as evidence for feudalisation (R.S. Sharma).

**The AP angle**
The very Chalukya king who stopped Harsha, **Pulakeshin II**, also overran the **Vishnukundins of Andhra** and installed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** as viceroy — founding the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** in coastal Andhra (c. 624 CE). So Harsha's Narmada check and the rise of a long-lived Andhra dynasty spring from the same Chalukya expansion — a neat link to AP history.

**Use in answers**
- Open by placing Harsha between the Guptas and early-medieval fragmentation (a bridge, not a new golden age).
- Quote one source (Harshacharita or Si-Yu-Ki) and the feudalisation debate for analytical depth.
- Diagram idea: a map-sketch with Kannauj at the centre and the Narmada as the hard southern line.

**TL;DR**
- Frame Harsha as the last north-Indian paramountcy, strong in culture, weak in structure.
- Carry datable facts (606, 618–619, 630–643, 647) and two named sources into the hall.
- Use the Pulakeshin II → Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi link for the AP angle.
keyPoints: Mains dimensions: rise/unification, limits (Narmada/Pulakeshin), culture, administration, nature & decline.
Quote sources: Harshacharita (Banabhatta), Si-Yu-Ki (Hiuen-Tsang), Aihole inscription.
Debate Harsha's state as a loose feudal paramountcy (land grants, few coins; R.S. Sharma).
AP angle: Pulakeshin II also founded the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in Andhra via Kubja Vishnuvardhana.
Answer tip: present Harsha as a bridge between the Guptas and early-medieval fragmentation.
